question: The Commission’s proposals on the defence industry1 underline the EU’s ambition to achieve full industrial and technological self-sufficiency in the field of defence by 2030.

The Commission places emphasis on the financing of European projects, the transfer of design rights and intellectual property to Member States and reducing dependence on allies outside the Union – even though it is precisely these allies, especially after the outbreak of full-scale war, who played a key role in the rapid rebuilding of the defence capabilities of many Member States, especially on the EU’s eastern flank.

At the same time, in the ‘Defence Readiness Roadmap 2030’, the Commission acknowledges that defence production depends on access to critical raw materials and that European industry is facing ‘strategic dependences and bottlenecks’ in this area. This situation is exacerbated by China’s decision in October to impose export restrictions on rare earth elements.

Such a policy raises doubts about the coherence of the EU’s strategy. By pushing for ‘strategic autonomy’, which may be perceived negatively by our allies, the EU maintains an actual dependence on raw materials controlled by a third country which NATO describes as a strategic rival. 1.
What specific measures is the Commission taking to end the EU’s dependence on supplies of rare earth minerals and other critical raw materials from China and to diversify its sources of supply?

Does the Commission plan to strengthen strategic partnerships with countries that have deposits of critical raw materials, such as Canada, Australia and Kazakhstan, in order to bolster the resilience of the European defence sector?
Defence Readiness Roadmap 2030, Security Action for Europe (SAFE), European Defence Industry Programme (EDIP) and the Defence Readiness Omnibus
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.1.2026) Critical raw materials (CRMs) dependencies undermine the EU’s long-term competitiveness and transition objectives. They also risk hampering its defence readiness targets and support to Ukraine, thereby posing a direct security risk and undermining European security.

EU institutions and Member States, in coordination with the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, should mobilise every possible lever at their disposal to expediently decrease CRMs dependencies from defence industrial value chains. The Commission takes seriously the risk stemming from dependency on China on the different stages of the raw materials process.

The Commission adopted the RESourceEU Action Plan on 3 December 20251. The aim of RESourceEU is to secure access to alternative sources of CRMs in the short, medium and long term for the European industry.

The RESourceEU Action Plan includes a proposal for a new financing hub that will de-risk investment and coordinate different aims of funding, as well as proposals of adjustments to the EU-regulatory framework on permitting. Work on CRMs partnerships with resource-rich countries will continue, as well as coordination with like-minded countries in relevant multilateral fora.
The above-mentioned avenues to address the CRMs dependencies’ risks are instrumental to strengthen defence capabilities, as well as defence readiness and industrial resilience by 2030.
